en: Preface to the *Zhuzhou Weishan Jingce*, composed by Zhang Zhu, Imperial Commissioner of the Left and Newly Appointed Transport Commissioner for the Eastern Route of Guangnan:
From the Sixth Patriarch downward, there were five lineages; the Weiyang lineage was one of them. Alas, that its transmission was not maintained thereafter.

The transmission [of this teaching] has endured for ten thousand generations without decay, its existence not dependent on any individual. The *Cautionary Verses* (Jingce) of Mount Weiyan is a prime example of this.
For the practice of these verses has long been current in the world; yet students have often lamented that although the phrasing is clear, their meaning is difficult to exhaustively fathom.
Furthermore, there were errors and corruptions in the characters that remained unresolved for a long time. Had it not been for a true Master...

How could a great master be able to propagate its meaning and correct its errors? Master Dahan Jingyan, whose Chan learning was preeminent in the world, would occasionally engage in writing during his leisure time.
In the year Jihwei (1359), while in retreat, he provided a commentary at the request of his students.
Its meaning is straightforward and clear; furthermore, as for the errors in the characters, they have been [corrected].

I have thus corrected it so that late learners and those of later generations may have a model to emulate, causing the traces of Mount Guiyang, which had been obscured for two hundred years, to suddenly shine forth once more.
To thereby transmit this work to infinity and bestow its benefits boundlessly—is this not indeed most appropriate?
The disciple Shi Dexian wished to carve it onto woodblocks to broaden its dissemination; I, admiring his resolve, have readily composed this preface for him.
Preface placed at the beginning of this volume. Respectfully written on the first day of the twelfth month in the ninth year of the Xiangxing era.
*Annotated Wuyun’s Admonition* (Miaoyan Jingce Zhu). Wuyun’s Admonition.
Annotated by the Chan Master Shousui, a Dharma-heir of Da Hongzhi.
The Master’s name was Lingyou.
Initially, he studied under Chan Master Baidai Dazhi. One night, while standing in attendance until late, Baidai said, "Move [the firewood]..."
[Zhuozi] looked into the brazier. The Master [Baizhang] pushed it aside and said, "There is no fire in the brazier.
Baizhang himself rose and probed deeply, whereupon he obtained a single spark of fire. Holding it up, he asked, "You say there is none; what is this? Through this, the Master attained realization.
Baizhang then instructed Sima Tuo to select a site on Mount Miao that was suitable for establishing a monastic center. He then said to the assembly, "If there were..."
Having obtained a turning word, Daowu went to reside at Guishan. Pointing to a water pitcher, he asked, "If you call it a 'water pitcher,' you commit the fault of attachment;
if you do not call it a 'water pitcher,' you commit the fault of aversion. At that time, Hualin was the Head Seat.
"Cloud" cannot be called a wooden mallet. The Master (Baizhang) did not agree. At that time, the Teacher (Dongshan) served as the head cook (*karmadāna*).
The Master then questioned the Teacher, who kicked over a pure water jar. The Master said, "The Head Seat has lost the mountain. The Teacher later resided at Mount Gui.

Having established the single school of the Guiyang lineage, his Way was transmitted throughout the world; he then composed the *Jingsce* (The Admonition) to warn those who have not yet awakened and to spur those who have not yet advanced.
For indeed, as karma binds one to receive a body, one cannot avoid the encumbrances of form.
Being the root of suffering, it is mentioned first so that one may awaken to the source of delusion; only then can one advance upon the Path.

These two characters, "karmic bondage" (ye-xi), arise from the initial movement of the mind of non-awakening, which is called the "phase of karma" (ye-xiang). This is followed by the "phase of transformation" (zhuan-xiang).
The subsequent manifestation of appearances constitutes the three subtle marks. From this manifestation of appearances arise the six coarse marks:
the mark of objective realms, the mark of continuity, the mark of grasping, the mark of calculating names and words, the mark of creating karma, and the mark of suffering bound by karma.
The first five [aspects] may still be countered through remedial measures; however, this final aspect—the characteristic of suffering that binds sentient beings—cannot be remedied.
Since this body is formed from the seeds and habitual tendencies of the three subtle and six coarse levels of ignorance, how can one escape its physical form and its burdensome constraints?
Having received this physical body as a legacy from one's parents, it is brought into being through the convergence of various conditions.
Because one receives consciousness and deluded thoughts, one takes birth within the red and white elements of the parents.

Relying on such conditions as nursing, bathing, food, drink, clothing, and shelter, the body is able to persist. The Buddha said: "Contemplate the impurity of the body; contemplate that sensation is suffering."
Although the four great elements support one another, they are constantly in opposition;
the internal earth, water, fire, and wind are each distinct in nature.
Impermanence, old age, and sickness do not wait for an appointment with anyone.
The four great elements and the five aggregates arise and perish from moment to moment;
they exist in the morning and vanish by evening. In a single kṣaṇa, one passes into another world.
A kṣaṇa is an extremely brief interval of time.
For example, like spring frost or morning dew, they vanish in an instant.
The mark of impermanence changes and perishes in a mere moment;
how could the trees on the bank or the vines by the well endure for long?
It is likewise with this body: fragile and impermanent.
Moments pass with such rapidity that in a single kṣaṇa, it is as if four powerful giants were simultaneously shooting arrows toward the four directions, while another person—
The time it takes to simultaneously draw back these four arrows is called a single *kṣaṇa*.
A single breath is already a future life; why then do you allow it to pass away in vain?

From the beginning of this chapter until this point, the passage has described the deluded body and the deluded world of both the layperson and the renunciant, demonstrating that impermanence is swift and rapid.
The faults and afflictions are thus; one must be cautioned and awakened so as not to let time pass in vain.
From this point forward, I shall describe only the causes and conditions for leaving the household life, so that each may reflect and examine themselves.
If parents are not provided with sweet delicacies, one's six kin will surely abandon them;
when all karmic ties are discarded, one merely returns to the ordinary and accords with the Way,
yet remains unable to bring peace to the state or govern the realm.
Having bid farewell to my parents and severed ties with my kin, I am yet unable to exhaust my devotion in serving the public, thereby bringing grace to the sovereign and benefit to the people.
What should I do? My family estate is suddenly abandoned, and the succession of my lineage is left unsecured.
To leave no lineage is unfilial; to leave the household life to propagate the Way is true great filial piety.

Distancing oneself from one's hometown and kin, shaving the head to receive the precepts from a teacher, suddenly abandoning worldly ties, and severing all emotional attachments—to shave the head and receive the precepts from a teacher is to practice the Great Way of the ancient Buddhas. This is identical [to the former].
Regarding the countenance and deportment of the ancient Buddhas:
internally, they diligently applied the power of mindfulness; externally, they propagated the virtue of non-contention.
To practice the meritorious deeds of renunciation, it is essential that one’s inner state and outer conduct be in accord.
To be utterly detached from the mundane world and aspire toward liberation—
keeping one's resolve fixed on escaping the secular realm— is precisely what accords with the profound intent of leaving home (*pravrajyā*).
Why, then, as soon as you have ascended to the level of the precepts, do you immediately declare, "I am a *bhikṣu*"?
To claim for oneself the title of "bhikṣu" while the marks of a self (ātman) manifest before one can be verified—
receiving what the donor requires, consuming the property of the monastic community (saṃgha),
wearing clothes without raising silkworms, and eating food without plowing— is [nothing more than hypocrisy].
Without understanding or reflecting upon the source from which food comes, a bhikṣu receiving food should perform the five contemplations.

He should contemplate its origin, calculate the labor expended, reflect that a single grain of rice required seventy-three cycles of effort according to the ancient masters, and weigh his own virtue against the requirements for such an offering. Thus he should realize [the gravity of his task].
Only an Arhat is truly entitled to the full title of "Worthy of Offerings" (Arhat); all others are termed "deficiently worthy of offerings.
To claim that one is naturally and rightfully entitled to such offerings is a false conceptualization born of emotional attachment; how can one possibly assess one's own faults?
Having gathered together, they chatter and clamor, speaking only of worldly trifles.

Having left the household life, one’s resolve should be to seek the Great Way of non-action; yet instead of investigating the words and intent of the Buddha, they conform to worldly conventions and engage in noisy tumult.
From this point downward, they forget their origin and deviate from their original purpose.
Thus, in the pursuit of pleasure for a single lifetime, one fails to realize that pleasure is the cause of suffering.
The pleasures of worldly convention are entirely the root of suffering; there is no doubt that receiving offerings from the faithful in vain constitutes a debt.
Even bearing an iron chain or a saddle is but a light retribution for such actions.
In past kalpas, you pursued the dust of the world without ever reflecting back;
throughout vast eons, you have followed after delusion and turned your back on awakening, never for a moment turning the light inward.
Time has slipped away and years have been wasted; your enjoyments have been abundant and your gains from offerings have been rich and thick.
Deluded by worldly gains, they have not yet examined themselves or turned their light inward;
though years and ages pass, they show no intent to renounce them,
remaining attached to their dwellings and unaware of their faults and afflictions.
Accumulations become ever more numerous;
one merely maintains this illusory substance, preserving only a phantom and delusive form that contravenes the pure *dharmakāya*.
The Teacher has issued a decree to exhort the bhikṣus: advance upon the Path and adorn your persons, for the three [requisites] are never sufficient.
The *Buddha’s Bequeathed Teaching Sūtra* states: First, one should rub one's own head to renounce ornaments and wear robes of dyed color;
holding an alms bowl, one should beg for food to sustain oneself. Second, when receiving food and drink from others, one should regard it as taking medicine;
whether it be good or bad, do not harbor feelings of preference or aversion. Obtain just enough to support the body and eliminate hunger and thirst, like a bee gathering nectar from flowers. Only...
One takes its flavor without damaging its color or fragrance; so it is with the bhikṣu. When receiving offerings from others, he should proceed only to remove his own afflictions;
he must not seek much, lest he destroy his wholesome mind. Third, during the day he should diligently practice wholesome dharmas without letting the time pass in vain;
during the first and last watches of the night he should likewise not neglect them; and during the middle watch of the night, he should recite the sūtras to rest and refresh himself.

Do not allow your entire life to pass in vain on account of sleep. That is to say, regarding food, clothing, and sleep—these three matters—one must know that they are not to be indulged in to one's heart's content, even if they are sufficient for one's needs.
Yet many people indulge in these things without ceasing.
"Flavor" refers to attachment.
As days pass and months come, one suddenly becomes white-haired.
An ancient said: "One only knows that affairs pass before one's eyes; one does not realize that old age creeps up from the head."
Those of later generations have not yet heard the essential meaning;
regarding the purpose of leaving the household life,
one must extensively consult those who possess prior knowledge.
One must not remain ignorant and self-satisfied, thinking that leaving the household life is merely for the sake of seeking food and clothing.

Those who have left the household life do so for the sake of the unconditioned Dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*); yet, out of private sentiments and foolish views, they conversely claim it is for the sake of seeking food and clothing.
The Buddha first established the Vinaya to initiate and enlighten the ignorant,
to awaken those in darkness,
and to provide the rules for dignified deportment.
Possessing a majestic presence worthy of reverence and a dignified demeanor worthy of emulation,
he is as pure as ice and snow;
unlike the heterodox practitioners whose mixed precepts are entirely impure.
Regarding the observance through cessation (*śīla*) and the transgression through action:

for the *saṃvara-śīla* (the precept of restraint), one restrains the initial mind; cessation of evil constitutes observance, while committing evil constitutes transgression. For the *kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla* (the precept of gathering virtuous dharmas), cessation of virtue constitutes transgression, while performing virtue constitutes observance.
The subtle precepts rectify all vulgar abuses;
the five sections and seven groups, comprising both natural and proscribed prohibitions, were not formulated until twelve years after the Buddha’s attainment of enlightenment.
Ānanda asked the Buddha why he had not established the precepts during the twelve years prior. The Buddha said, "It is like mending a garment in the world:
if the garment is not yet torn, mending it will only invite criticism. I am likewise; I establish the precepts based on specific circumstances. Thus it was said.
I have never had the honor of participating in a formal assembly for the Vinaya; how then could I possibly discern the *nītārtha* (definitive meaning) of the Supreme Vehicle?

"Vinaya" refers to the study of the precepts. One gives rise to meditative concentration (*samādhi*) because of the precepts, and one develops wisdom (*prajñā*) because of meditative concentration. Yet, even in the study of the Vinaya, I remain ignorant of the definitive meaning.
How can one possibly fathom its profound meaning?
It is a pity that a lifetime will pass in vain; regret is difficult to undo once it has arisen.
If one does not exert oneself in youth, there will be nothing accomplished in old age. What benefit is there in feeling remorse later on?
I have never applied my mind to the principles of the teachings, and thus there is no cause for me to realize the profound Way.
Since I have not yet turned my attention toward the logical systems of the holy teachings, how could I possibly realize the mysterious and subtle Way?
As they reach advanced age and long standing in the order, their bellies remain empty while their hearts grow haughty; they refuse to draw near to virtuous friends and know only to be arrogant.
Possessing years but lacking virtue, they protect their shortcomings and gloss over their errors. Ignorance has become habitual, and they remain loftily self-important.
Unfamiliar with the Vinaya, they lack any sense of restraint.
Not associating with virtuous friends, how could they know the Vinaya? Their three karmas and four modes of conduct constantly deviate from the regulations;
they speak loudly and in high voices, uttering words without moderation.
They lack all restraint and self-discipline; this pertains to the bodily action (*kāyakarman*). They speak loudly and with a high voice; this pertains to the vocal action (*vākkarman*).
They show no respect toward seniors, equals, or juniors; they are no different from a gathering of Brahmins.
Lack of respect is a matter of mental karma (*manas-karma*). According to the Vinaya, there are three grades—superior, middling, and inferior.

The Buddha ordained that those who received the precepts first are senior, while those who received them later are junior; this is not the case among non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). From this point onward, [the text] proceeds to successively admonish them regarding their transgressions.
The bowls and basins made a sound. Having finished eating, he was the first to rise.
"Wan" (椀) is the Chinese term; "po" (鉢) is a Sanskrit word, fully called *pātra*. In this land, it is translated as "measured vessel."
If one makes a sound, fire arises in the throats of the hungry ghosts;
their movements are discordant, and they entirely lack the nature of the *saṃgha*.
"Saṃgha" in its full Sanskrit form is *saṃghāya*; this is translated here as "the harmony of the assembly. It refers to the harmony of both principle (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*).
Regarding the essence of a monk (*saṃgha-tva*): since one’s conduct in coming and going is not in accordance with the Dharma, what essence of a monk can there be?

To cause others’ minds to be startled and agitated when rising or sitting—“startled” (*chōng*) here meaning that the spirit and mind are unsettled—one who causes distress to others by leaving the household life is not called a *śramaṇa*.
If we do not preserve these minor rules of conduct and slight points of decorum, with what means shall we restrain future generations? New learners will have no basis upon which to model themselves.
If one cannot practice right conduct oneself, it is impossible for one to cause others to practice it;
as soon as they are observed, they immediately claim, "I am a mountain monk."
Arrogant regarding self and others, he oppressed those junior to him in learning.
Having never heard the Buddhist teachings or practiced them, his mind was consistently coarse;
his conduct and understanding were devoid of merit, while he was thoroughly proficient only in worldly conventions.
Such a view arises because those at the beginning stage are indolent and negligent; they are gluttonous and habituated to following their impulses.
To crave wealth is called *tāo* (greed), and to crave food is called *tiē* (gluttony).
As time slips away amidst the world, one eventually becomes coarse and uncultivated.
As the years slip away in the midst of worldly dust, how could one recognize the tranquility of leisure?
Unaware, one becomes decrepit and aged; in every encounter, one is like someone facing a wall.
"Lung-chung" (躘蹱) describes the manner of walking without progress; "facing a wall" means to be utterly ignorant of all things.
When later students come to inquire, you receive them with silence.
Since your own wisdom is not yet clear, how can you awaken those who are junior?
Even if you do speak, your words will not touch upon the scriptural teachings.
To speak recklessly from mere conjecture is to invite derision from onlookers.
If one is lightly criticized, they immediately reproach the younger generation for their lack of propriety;
failing to reflect upon their own faults, they instead blame the transgressions of others.
When a mind of anger arises and resentment flares up, one’s words strike others.

With the arising of a single thought of anger, a million gates of obstruction open. Once the three poisons run rampant through ordinary sentiments, how could one ever contemplate the Buddha’s words of the Four Truths?
One morning, he lay ill upon his bed, entangled and oppressed by manifold sufferings. From dawn until dusk he brooded over them, his mind filled with agitation;
thus, pressed by these various pains, he was agitated, terrified, and anxious.
The path ahead is vast and obscure; I know not where it leads.
I have vainly presided over this illusory body; how could I have awakened to the true home?
From this moment forth, I begin to know my transgressions. What is the use of digging a well when one is already thirsty?
Even if one repents and recognizes one's faults, by what means can one accomplish meritorious practice?
One laments that one did not cultivate earlier; now, in old age, many transgressions abound.
Once the transgressions have become manifest, what benefit is there in repenting?
As the moment of departure approaches,
one squanders [one's merit]; lacking the power of meditative concentration, one meekly submits to the gateway of death,
trembling with fear and terror.
There is no goodness upon which to rely, and no virtue to which one can turn for refuge.
When the silk is torn and the sparrow flies out, consciousness follows along with karma.
As the *Saptakumārikā-sūtra* states: "A sparrow enters a jar and covers its opening with silk; when the silk is torn, the sparrow flies away."
Go! The conscious mind follows along with karma, just as when a person has debts, the stronger creditor drags them away first.
The power of good and evil karma all takes deluded consciousness as its master; whichever force is strongest drags one away, leaving no room for personal autonomy.
The mind's tendencies are manifold; it falls toward that which is most weighty.
Within the six realms and four modes of birth, one receives retribution according to one's own thoughts and attachments.
The demon of impermanence slays without ceasing, moment after moment.
That which arises is simultaneously subject to cessation; this is not taught to the foolish.
Life cannot be extended.
As it was said of old: "If impermanence arrives at dusk, it will not wait for you until the first watch."
Time cannot be waited for.
Do not say, "I will not study today, for there is tomorrow," or "I will not study this year, for there is next year.
Alas, when one has grown old, whose fault is it?
As for humans, devas, and the three realms of existence, one should not expect to escape them;
the three worlds offer no peace, being like a house on fire.
To receive such a body is not a matter of merely counting kalpas.
Like the buckets of a well-drawing wheel, rising and falling in alternation, he was moved to lament and wonder; alas, how piercing was his heart!
Miaoshan grieved that [his disciples] had not yet awakened, his feelings being so urgent.
How could one remain silent? We must exhort and admonish one another.

Sentient beings wander through the realms of suffering, clutching their treasures while lost in their own lands. Since you are a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), how can you remain mute and fail to inspire them?
What I regret is that we were born together in this age of semblance-dharma (*sāṃketika-dharma*), when our distance from the Sage is vast.
This age of semblance-dharma refers to the two thousand years following the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa; this is the time for creating exhortations.
Now, more than two hundred years have passed, and our distance from the Sage grows ever greater.
The Buddha-dharma has become superficial; people are mostly indolent, and their faculties are all inferior. How can this be compared to the time of the Buddha’s True Dharma?
I briefly set forth my humble views to enlighten those who come after.
Mount Gui’s humble words—that his insight was like looking at the sky through a tube—were intended merely to instruct later students.
If one does not eliminate self-conceit, it is truly difficult to escape;
if one does not eliminate the faults of prior arrogance and self-praise, it is indeed difficult to evade the suffering of karmic retribution.

[This is] the wheel. Yongjia said: "To eliminate self-importance and indolence, to disregard the physical form, and to single-mindedly preserve the ultimate Way—can this not be called attuning the spirit within the square inch of the heart?

From here below, there is a separate account of the fundamental intention for resolving to leave the household life, visiting wise teachers and drawing near to spiritual friends to clarify the causal conditions of the Great Matter, and finally practicing through the successive periods of the Buddha’s dispensation.
The teaching of the Buddha’s Heart-Mind Essence must require the correspondence of practice and understanding; this is the beginning and end of continuing the Buddha’s life of wisdom.
Now, as for those who have left the household life, they set out with their feet toward the transcendent realm, their minds and bodies differing from the mundane world.
Walking alone upon the Great Path, his mind transcends worldly sorrow;
he upholds and flourishes the lineage of the Sages, shaking and subduing the armies of Māra;
his resolve is equal to that of the Buddhas of antiquity, and his power overcomes all demons.
To repay the four debts of gratitude—
the debt to the Buddha, the debt to the king, the debt to one's parents, and the debt to patrons—
and to deliver beings from the three realms of existence.
The realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm constitute the sentient beings of the three worlds.
If one does not act accordingly, one improperly joins the ranks of the monastic community;
conversely, if one acts otherwise, one is entirely confused and impure, and is no longer a son of the Śākya.
My conduct and speech have become negligent and coarse; I have received offerings of faith in vain.
Such offerings are intended for the field of merit, yet through negligence, they benefit neither myself nor others.
As for the places where I once practiced, not a single step has been moved from them.
An ancient said: "Only change the path you have traveled; do not change the person you were.
If one's entire life passes in a blur, what can one rely upon?
If it is all like a dream from which one has not yet awakened, what merit or practice can be relied upon?
How much more so for one who possesses the majestic appearance of a monk, whose countenance is worthy of admiration; such a dignified bearing is not easily attained.
It is entirely due to the cultivation of roots of goodness in past lives that one receives such extraordinary retribution.
The causes of this present life were sown in previous lives; the fruits of the future are cultivated in this present life.
To then sit upright with hands folded, deeming not even a moment of time precious—this is to misunderstand the ancients who valued a single inch of time more than a foot-long jade disc.
If one is not diligent in their practice, the fruits of merit cannot be achieved through causes.
The Buddhas of antiquity passed through three incalculable eons, giving rise to the four great vows and cultivating myriad practices;

with both merit and wisdom fully adorned, every subtle flaw and obscuration exhausted and not a single fragment of goodness left behind, they finally realized the fruit of Buddhahood. How could an ordinary person possibly be so complete?

If one does not diligently cultivate the training in ethical discipline, concentration, and wisdom while yet desiring to seek the unsurpassed, supreme fruit, how can one possibly allow this single lifetime to pass in vain? Moreover, it would likewise fail to benefit one's future karma.
Not only will you have brought your own life to ruin, but there will be no refuge for your future rebirths either.
Having bid farewell to your kin and resolved to don the saffron robes, where do you intend to transcend all equally?
What is the fundamental purpose of your renunciation?
Morning and night I reflect: how could I allow time to pass by idly?
Retreating to contemplate within myself, I shall advance in my studies while I am in good health, aspiring to become a pillar of the Buddha-dharma and serving as a mirror for future generations.
The courageous will aspires to be a pillar of the Buddha-dharma; the model of conduct serves as a tortoise-shell and mirror for later students.
The tortoise foretells future fortune and calamity; the mirror reflects present beauty and ugliness.
It has always been thus; one has not yet attained even a small degree of correspondence with it.
Although there is aspiration, practice and understanding are not yet sufficient; therefore, it is said that one has "not yet" [attained it].
When speaking, one must engage with the classical texts and precedents.
Speech that does not accord with the classics is not the discourse of a gentleman.
Discourse should instead be grounded in the investigation of antiquity;
for words are the sprouts of the mind—how could they be the reckless pronouncements of one’s own breast or groundless talk lacking historical verification?
His physical appearance was exceptionally distinguished; his form was upright and his countenance correct.
His spirit and demeanor were lofty and serene.
When a river possesses pearls, the river becomes beautiful; when a person harbors the Way, they become lofty and serene.
On a long journey, one must rely on a good companion, for their company repeatedly purifies one’s ears and eyes.
The Buddha asked Ānanda, "To what extent does a virtuous friend constitute the holy life (*brahmacarya*)? Ānanda replied, "It constitutes half of the holy life. The Buddha said:

Not so. A virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra) is one who completes the holy life (brahmacarya). Furthermore, it is said in antiquity: "When three people walk together, there must be someone among them whom I can take as my teacher;
I shall select what is good in them and follow it."
In dwelling and practicing, one must necessarily choose one's companions. From time to time, one hears what has not been heard before;
this brings forth what was previously unheard and awakens those who are deluded—all of which is the power of one’s fellow practitioners on the Path.
Therefore it is said: "Those who give birth to me are my parents; those who bring me to fulfillment are my friends.

Those who share the same gate are called *peng* (companions); those who share the same aspiration are called *you* (friends). Parents can give birth to the physical body (*rūpakāya*), but they cannot cause one to transcend the evil realms.

Only the spiritual benefactor (*kalyāṇamitra*) establishes the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), opens up true and correct knowledge and vision, and enables one to enter the ranks of the sages and transcend the mundane.
How could one possibly neglect the grace of its generation?
To associate with the virtuous is like walking through mist and dew; though it does not soak one's clothes, it provides moisture from time to time.
A virtuous friend as a companion nourishes the roots of goodness; its benefit is immeasurable.
Associating with the wicked leads to the growth of evil knowledge and views; one commits evil morning and night, receiving immediate retribution in this very life.
By befriending those who are not true friends and following deviant ways and evil, one violates the laws of the king and becomes loathed and despised by others.
After death, one sinks into the depths of suffering; once the human body is lost, it will not be regained for ten thousand kalpas.
Influenced by evil friends, one commits irrational acts; in life, one encounters the king’s law, and in death, one enters the Avīci Hell.
Loyal words are contrary to the ear; how could one not engrave them in one's heart?
Bitter-tasting, loyal speech must indeed be contrary to the ear; upon hearing it, one should rectify one's faults and engrave them deeply within the heart.
Thus one is able to cleanse the mind and nurture virtue; to obscure one's traces and conceal one's fame.
By cleansing the mind, the mind becomes pure; by nurturing virtue, virtue becomes full. By obscuring one's traces, one harmonizes with the light and blends with the dust;
by concealing empty fame, one discards the flowery to pursue the substantial.
The essence of his spirit was refined; clamor and bustle were brought to an end.

He nurtured his nature in serene seclusion, remaining pure, leisurely, and free from anxiety. Herein, first the account of his studies is related, followed by the account of his mastery of the teachings.
If you wish to engage in Chan and study the Way, suddenly transcending the gates of expedient means,
you must directly abandon expedients and speak only of the Unsurpassed Way,
so that your mind may accord with the profound ford.
The mind has no divergent objects;
it investigates the subtle and the exquisite.
It researches all dharmas, penetrating to the ultimate subtlety and excellence.
He discerned the profound and deep,
exploring the obscure and seeking out the hidden; he resolved what was subtle and minute,
opening up the awakening to the true source.
To open the source of the profound truth of reality, one must consult widely with those who possess prior knowledge.
One should not remain in a dark room guarding ignorance and delusion; rather, one ought to study extensively to support and cultivate meditative concentration and wisdom.
Draw near to virtuous friends.
Sudhana’s southern journey to seek out his friends brought his lifelong study of the Way to completion. An ancient said: "The clear and correct is the South;
when the directions are exhausted, it is the South. To take me as a friend—let all people take me as a friend. Encountering the three poisons, the three virtues become perfect. Entering...
In a single speck of dust, one’s mind becomes tranquil; this accords with Mañjuśrī’s wondrous wisdom.
It is precisely the original mind entering the profound gate of Samantabhadra, never having possessed a separate essence. This may be called drawing near to a virtuous friend. As the Book says:
"Toward those who are good toward me, I am also good; toward those who are evil toward me, I am also evil. How much more so for a son of the Śākya?
The subtlety of this school is difficult to attain; one must apply oneself with meticulous care.
If this Dharma-gate of the mind-ground is realized within the mind, then even *eranda* weeds become *candana* sandalwood trees.
If its essential meaning is lost, then even nectar becomes a garden of thorns. How could it be easy to approach with a coarse mind?
Within this, one may suddenly awaken to the True Cause; this is precisely the gradual progression for transcending the mundane world.
If one suddenly awakens to these two words, "True Cause," then the hundred rivers will merge into the sea without distinguishing their sources and flows.

When a single thought accords with reality, the boundaries of past and future are severed. The essence of illumination stands alone; both self and objects are thus. One transcends worldly toil; as for the principle—
In the vehicle of sudden enlightenment, delusion is extinguished simultaneously with awakening; yet phenomena are not suddenly eliminated, for they are exhausted through a gradual process.
This refers to the destruction of the twenty-five states of existence within the three realms.
As the Treatise says: "The four continents, the four evil destinies, the Brahma kings, the six heavens of desire, the Heaven of No-Thought, the Pure Abodes, and the four formless realms."
Together with the four dhyānas, these constitute the twenty-five realms of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*).
One thoroughly realizes that all internal and external phenomena are unreal; they arise through transformations of the mind and are entirely provisional designations (*prajñapti*).

The internal mind and external objects are false and unsubstantial, all being transformations of deluded consciousness. If one awakens to the fact that the triple world is mind-only, [one is liberated].
All phenomena are but consciousness. Within the light of tranquil illumination, nothing can be apprehended.
There is no need to apply the mind to settle it;
for to employ the mind by means of the mind—is this not a great error?
It is simply that emotion does not adhere to objects; how could objects obstruct the person?
When emotion is false and not true, objects are fundamentally not objects.
Let the nature of dharmas flow freely as it will; neither sever it nor continue it.
There is no need to sever delusion to continue with truth; the nature of phenomena flows everywhere in its own accord.
Hearing sounds and seeing forms are merely the ordinary course of things.
Yet these very sights and sounds are not "seeing and hearing"; there are no other sounds or forms to be presented to you. If one understands this completely within it—
There is no objective reality. Essence and function may be distinguished or not, yet whether on this side or that, their application is never lacking.
From the empty kalpa to the present moment, principle and phenomena are without separation; without leaving the site of enlightenment, one travels throughout all lands within the dust motes.
To conduct oneself in such a manner is truly not to wear the dharma robes in vain.
When practice and understanding are correct, and the internal and external correspond,
one thereby repays the four debts of gratitude and delivers beings from the three realms of existence.
The Way of Universal Salvation brings benefit to both self and others.
If one can never regress in this process of perpetual birth, the stage of Buddhahood may certainly be expected.
Treading upon this profound path requires more than just one or two lifetimes; with every step, one ascends the ladder of the Buddhas, never again to fall back.

He turns [the wheel of Dharma]. A guest who comes and goes through the three realms, appearing and disappearing to serve as an example for others, the Buddha is the guide of the three realms. As a sutra says: "Now these three realms are all mine; within them, the multitudes..."
All those born are my children. Having practiced the Way of the Ancient Buddhas, I act as a model for sentient beings, leading them to transcendence.
This single study is most wondrous and most profound; if you simply possess a resolute mind, you will certainly not be deceived.

The Patriarch came from the West to point directly to the human mind, so that one may see one's nature and become a Buddha. This method for transcending the mundane and entering the sacred is certainly unfailing;

it is only feared that students will be unwilling to apply their minds. If they are as if existing and yet as if non-existent, or advancing and yet retreating, then they cannot penetrate into the realization.
From this point onward, we shall separately address the various capacities of the faculties and thoroughly investigate the meaning of the teachings.
If there are those of middling capacity who are unable to transcend suddenly, they should for the time being devote their minds to the teachings and study the palm-leaf manuscripts.
Since spiritual capacities are not uniform, separate gates of expedient means are opened. To warm up the old and know the new, one must necessarily follow the finger to see the moon.
Thoroughly investigate the principles and meanings, transmit and propagate them, guide future generations, and repay the Buddha’s kindness;
in this way, time will not be wasted, and you must certainly rely upon this for support.
To transmit the teachings and guide the deluded, one must possess the eye of the Dharma; therefore, it is said that one must support oneself by means of this.
One who abides in the proper deportment is truly a vessel of the Dharma within the Sangha.
His dignified deportment was solemn and still, and his every movement was worthy of admiration. Only when one’s inner virtue is fully cultivated does one become a vessel for the Dharma.
Have you not seen how the climbing vine upon the pine tree soars to a height of a thousand fathoms? It is only by relying on a superior cause that it can bring about such vast benefit.
The preceding analogy follows from the Dharma. The ancients said: "The green ivy, through causes and conditions, climbs straight to the summit of the cold pine;
by means of internal causes and external conditions mutually supporting one another, it finally attains the unsurpassed fruit and extensively benefits all sentient beings."
Diligently cultivate the fast and precepts; do not allow them to be neglected or transgressed.
"Neglected" means deficient; "transgressed" means overstepped.
Through every generation and every lifetime, there will be most wondrous causes and effects.
Cause and effect are clearly manifest;
one must not pass the days in negligence or let time slip away in a state of dull stagnation. It is a great pity to waste this precious light of life by failing to seek spiritual advancement.
If you skillfully employ your mind, you will obtain a portion of the Buddha-dharma.

In vain one consumes the offerings of faith from the ten directions, which were bestowed for the sake of supporting one's path-practice. If the path-practice is not accomplished, how can one justify such consumption?
Furthermore, it would be a betrayal of the four debts of gratitude.
To sink into such depravity is to bring oneself to ruin and to betray one's own nature.
As these accumulations deepen, the dust of the mind easily becomes clogged.
With each passing day, transgressions grow deeper and heavier; the filth and grime of the mind block the source of spiritual clarity.
When the skeletal remains become stagnant, one is treated with contempt and deceit by others.

When the faculties and their objects are blocked and obstructed, one’s understanding and practice become perverse. Turning one’s back on the fundamental and pursuing the peripheral, one is held in low esteem by others.
As the ancients said: "Since he is a man of stature, so am I. One should not disparage oneself and succumb to despondency.
The teaching says: "The bodhisattvas of the worlds in the ten directions, in every thought-moment, strive toward the fruit of the Sugata.
Since they are great beings (puruṣa), so am I; I should not disparage myself and become disheartened."
If it were not so, one would merely remain within the monastic community for an entire life, passing the time in vain without any particular benefit.
It is better to practice as described above; then one will be able to realize the principle.
I humbly hope that you will rouse a resolute will and open a magnanimous mind. Let your actions be modeled after those of the superior;
do not arbitrarily follow the vulgar and base.
When you see the worthy, think of emulating them; when you see the unworthy, examine yourself within.
In this life, one must reach a definitive resolution. It is evident that this does not depend on others;
one must observe for oneself what is good and what is evil, for no one can take one's place.
One should quiet the mind and forget all external conditions.
Internally withdrawing the breath and externally forgetting all conditions,
one does not confront the various sensory objects.
If there is no internal movement, there is nothing to be done externally.
The mind is empty and the environment is still.
The mind is fundamentally empty; the environment is fundamentally still.
It is only because one has long been obstructed and stuck that they do not pass through.
Confused and obscured since beginningless time, you have turned your back on awakening and joined with the sensory dust.
Read this text thoroughly and use it to exhort yourself from time to time;
awaken through this text and alert your mind through it.
Exert yourself to maintain mastery; do not succumb to human sentiments.
When human sentiments are thick, the sentiment for the Way is thin;
being dragged by the fruits of one's karma, it is truly difficult to escape.
Calamities wrought by Heaven may still be escaped; those wrought by oneself cannot be avoided.
As sound is harmonized by resonance and form is made upright by its shadow, the retribution of cause and effect is like that of a shadow following a form or an echo responding to a sound.
Since the causal roots are clearly manifest, how could there be no anxiety or fear?
One who understands the Dharma fears;
thus, the Sūtra says:
As stated in the Sarvāstivāda sūtras:
"Even if one were to pass through hundreds of thousands of kalpas, the karma one has created does not perish. When the causes and conditions converge, one must experience the retribution oneself."

Because karma created due to delusion follows one like a shadow follows a form, once the fruits of that karma have ripened, they must be experienced even before the fruit of the noble path has been realized.
Thus, one knows that the punishments and entanglements of the triple world kill;
the constraints of the triple world are like a prison.
Exert yourselves in diligent cultivation; do not let the days pass in vain.
If every thought is not deluded, that is true cultivation; do not let them pass in vain.
Only by deeply understanding the faults and afflictions can you truly exhort one another to practice and uphold [the Dharma].

"One who seeks to deliver others before they have themselves attained deliverance" refers to the initial resolve of a Bodhisattva. "One whose own awakening is perfected and who then delivers others" refers to a Tathāgata appearing in the world.
Master Miu-shan himself recognized that the afflictions of sentient beings within the triple realm are such as these, and was further able to exhort others to practice accordingly;
how could one who has not reached such a stage be capable of this? Next, he provides the vow of proof.
May we be dharma companions together in every place throughout hundreds and thousands of kalpas and births.
Believe these words; practice these deeds. All such are companions of the Buddha-dharma.
Thus, he composed this inscription:
This is a summary verse reiterating the general purport of the preceding exhortations:
the illusory body and the dream-house;
that is, the illusory body composed of the four great elements and the dream-house of the triple world.
Examining the phenomena within space,
they are as unreal as flowers in the sky;
the prior limit is infinite, so how could the subsequent limit ever be reached?
Delusive phenomena cannot be found within the three periods of time.
Emerging here and submerging there, they exhaust themselves through rising and sinking;
their emergence and disappearance within birth and death have no fixed location. "Rising" refers to the realms of humans and devas; "sinking" refers to the miserable destinies.
One cannot yet escape the three wheels; when will there be rest?
Within the three realms, beings circulate like ants in a wheel, revolving without end.
Clinging to the world, the five aggregates (*skandhas*) and the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) form their substance.
There are three kinds of worlds: the world of the perfectly enlightened ones (*jñānasambuddha-loka*), the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*), and the world of the vessel (*bhājana-loka*).
This treatise concerns deluded attachment to the world of sentient beings and the world of the vessel; it does not refer to the world of the perfectly enlightened ones.
From birth until old age, one attains nothing at all;
delusive phenomena are fundamentally empty.
Due to this fundamental ignorance, one is thereby deluded.

Fundamental wisdom is permeated by ignorance; thus, the true follows along with the delusive. One falsely identifies the four great elements as the body and the shadows conditioned by the six sense-objects as the mind.

Grasping at a self and grasping at phenomena, one calculates intimacy and estrangement, and clings to names such as love and hatred. The creation of karma and the undergoing of retribution are all caused by the delusions of ignorance.
Time is to be cherished; not even a single kṣaṇa can be predicted.

Since birth and death occur in every kṣaṇa, one must not waste time. If one does not advance upon the path of the ancient Buddhas, this present life will pass in vain and the next life will be obstructed.
It is not merely that one life has been spent in vain; upon what can one rely for future realization?
To go from delusion to further delusion is entirely due to the six thieves.

These thieves of the six consciousnesses plunder the family treasure themselves. If one awakens to the eight consciousnesses, they can be transformed into the four wisdoms. As for the first five consciousnesses...

The wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*) corresponds to the sixth consciousness; the wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*) corresponds to the seventh consciousness;

the wisdom of equality (*samatā-jñāna*) corresponds to the seventh consciousness; and the great perfect mirror wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) corresponds to the eighth consciousness. Thus, with wisdom as the precursor for all six gates, what delusion could possibly exist?
Wandering back and forth through the six realms and crawling about within the three worlds—by what means can one escape from these three worlds and six realms?
Seek out an enlightened teacher at once; draw near to those of high virtue.
Seek out enlightened teachers and friends to be shown the essentials of true liberation;
discern body and mind to clear away their thorns;
clarify the mind and reach the fundamental source to eliminate all that is false and delusive.
The world is inherently floating and void; how could the myriad conditions ever constrain it?

Having realized that the four great elements, the sense faculties and their objects, and the three periods of time are without reality, and that all sufferings are empty, one should investigate the principles of the Dharma, taking awakening as the standard.
Having thoroughly investigated the source and origin, one suddenly awakens to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Mind and objects are both discarded; there is nothing to record and nothing to remember.
Inner mind and outer objects are released into their natural state; in essence, there is neither going nor staying.
The six sense faculties are serene; whether walking or standing, one remains in silent stillness.
With the joy of Dharma and the bliss of dhyāna, one moves and rests with effortless spontaneity. Within the four modes of deportment, calming (śamatha) and insight (vipaśyanā) proceed in tandem.
When the single mind does not arise, the myriad dharmas are simultaneously stilled.
When not a single thought arises, all conditions are suddenly stilled. Only at the final phrase does one reach the secure barrier;
the vital ford is cut off, allowing passage neither to the mundane nor the sagely. Who is the one who knows this? There is no need to recall Layman Pang any further;
in heaven and on earth, he alone knows it himself.
Commentary on the *Miaoguo Jingce* (Concluded):

The Way has neither past nor present; it is people who experience awakening or delusion. Therefore, the Elder Śākyamuni, relying on the power of his vows, manifested at the Deer Park and along the Bahudhika River in over three hundred assemblies.
Through speech that is beyond words, he revealed the truth to humans and devas, causing each to...

One enters into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Among these, only the *Sūtra in Forty-two Sections* and the *Sūtra on the Bequeathed Teachings* constitute the precious Dharma of instruction from beginning to end.
During the Yongping era of the Later Han dynasty, Kāśyapa Mātanga and Zhu Falan brought the former sūtra to the East;

its efficacy was verified by fire, and it established both the teachings and the school. Furthermore, during the Datong era of the Liang dynasty, twenty [sūtras] were obtained from the Western Heaven.
The Eighth Patriarch, Master Bodhidharma, transmitted the Buddha’s mind-seal. His previous direct pointing accords with the scriptures;

this is a great fortune for those among the people of our land who possess the capacity for the Mahāyāna. As for Master Huineng, he stood in the snow and severed his arm to seek instruction in the wondrous Way.
Upon hearing a single word, he attained awakening. He attended the Master for several years, and after three prostrations, he "attained the marrow. Thus was the transmission bestowed.

The robe and alms bowl were transmitted through seven generations until they reached Baizhang. Baizhang encountered Huangbo Yun and Guishan Lingyou, who greatly revitalized the profound tradition and added luster to the Buddha-sun.

Because Guishan observed that among his students there was little freedom from negligence, he subsequently composed *fayu* (Dharma discourses) to warn those who had not yet awakened and to spur those who had not yet reached the goal.
His writings were concise and his language direct; their meaning was vast and their intent profound. Within the monastic community...
The *Sūtra in Forty-two Sections*, the *Sūtra of the Buddha’s Bequeathed Teachings*, and the *Cautionary Admonitions of Mount Wei* are known as the "Three Sutras of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
One who can read through these directly and with immediate comprehension may become a Buddha or a Patriarch without passing through many lifetimes.

During the Xuande era, I further obtained Master Sui’s direct commentary on their profound meanings; it is marvelous how easy it is for beginners to understand! From this point on, those with aspirations toward [the Way]...
The Way requires far less effort than one might imagine. Without carrying incense, one beholds the Buddhas and Patriarchs; without moving a step, one ascends the site of enlightenment.
Now, the Great Master Hui of Jingshan has extracted the funds for his robes to carve this work into woodblocks at the Xiuxiu Hermitage in the region of Wu, so as to broaden its dissemination.

How marvelous! To carve into woodblocks by means of wealth is called the "gift of wealth"; to transmit the Dharma by means of teaching is called the "gift of Dharma. Thus, both wealth and Dharma are bestowed.
"This gift is called the Great Gift. The Buddha said, "One who can practice the Great Gift will certainly realize Bodhi.
In the future, Jingshan shall attain the perfect clarity of the Knowledge of All Modes (Sarvajñajñāna), and the Ten Epithets shall all be manifested; this is due to these excellent conditions.

Those who read this sutra should instead purify their minds like empty space. Before even unrolling the scroll, you must cast your gaze upon it, overturning habitual patterns and penetrating the profound mysteries. [He] pulled—
The wind of returning to truth is blowing; this is the final stage of the Great Vehicle's decline. If you perceive the righteous path and act with courage, you may yet become a vessel for the future.
Should you instead merely follow the traces of calligraphy and the lines of ink, you will surely bring great shame upon the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
The Lantern Festival of the *Ciming* Year of the *Zhizhi* Cycle (1286) was cut short. Recorded by the Herdsman Elder De’i. Preface to the Explanation:
Regarding the patrons, the Kim family—Jikpung, Jido, and Kowon—it is said that their great undertaking was the re-engraving of the Three Scriptures of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
They requested that I provide a colophon for them. I examined these texts: they are the *Sutra of Forty-two Sections* and the *Sutra of the Bequeathed Teachings*.
This is the *Cautionary Admonition* (Jingce) of Master Guishan. Its establishment of principles and creation of regulations leave not even the slightest detail unaddressed;
the direct path to becoming a Buddha or a Patriarch lies herein. How immeasurable must be the Dharma-gift bestowed by Elder Dao!

Students should regard this text as a stern master presiding above them, examining themselves with such urgency that they feel they cannot keep up. If they do not act thus, then even the Three Scriptures will be but empty words. How could it be otherwise?
How precious it is!
Written on the [blank] day of the tenth month of the Qīnglóng jiǎzǐ year.
Postscript by Yi Sŏk, Grand Master of the Third Order, Duke of Hansan, Meritorious Subject for Loyal Devotion and Preservation of Integrity, Co-Administrator of Virtue and Aider of Transformation.
The first two sutras were spoken by the Buddha; the latter, the *Jingsce* (Warning and Admonition), was spoken by Master Guishan.

These three scriptures are truly the fundamental pathways for serious students to enter the Way, engage in study, and become Buddhas and Patriarchs. Master Sui composed a commentary on them, which is like adding branches to the trunk. Master Jingshan did not do so;
he swept away the wild branches and leaves and carved them into woodblocks to propagate their transmission widely. This is because...
If one desires that every person should shoulder to shoulder and foot to foot with the Buddhas and Patriarchs, sharing the same experience, such a mind is indeed noble.
Should students be able to follow and practice this, then the Buddhas and Patriarchs are you, and you are the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
Yet, if even one or two individuals, as soon as they emerge from the mother’s womb, possess the strategic means to transcend both Buddhas and Patriarchs, then this sutra is for them alone.
A supplementary note.
Written with reverence by the monk Juegen Yida during the first half of spring in the year Bingxu.
